About this page

  • In this page we review the literature which document the development of Adela’s cfMeDIP-seq Technology. The source of all the information contained therein is public.


1 AI Reports

  • AI reports are produced by claude.ai Opus 4.5 with naive prompts from Francois Collin.

  • The reporting done is intended to provide the information needed to understand the roots and development of Adela’s cfMeDIP-seq Technology.


1.1 Adela vs GRAIL

  • A fairly comprehensive, high level comparison of the two platforms.

  • This compilation is for background purposes - see the documentation below for comments on technical aspects of some of the studies cited.


1.2 cfMeDIP-seq: Protocol, Pipeline and Classifiers

  • The evolution of Adela’s cfMeDIP-seq Protocol, Pipeline and Classifiers is traced.
  • The report is a fairly comprehensive, high level description of the assay and algorithm along with a description of enhancements that followed.


1.3 The utility of spike-in controls

  • _spike_in_normalization_cfMeDIP_report
    • Puts the general framework for spike-in normalization from Chen et al. (2015) [1] with the specifics of cfMeDIP-seq to rationalize the appoach in Wilson et al. (2022) [2].
  • _Wilson_2022_Spike_in_Controls_Technical_Review
    • contents of the paper are detailed.
    • Figures
  • _Wilson_2022_Critical_Analysis_Biological_Validation
    • points out that Wilson et al. (2022) [2] provides little evidence of the benefits of the spike-in normaliozation over alternatives,

1.3.1 Published Data

GEO Accession GSE166259:

  • Raw HCT116 cell line data (public)
  • Processed AML patient data (public)

EGA Accession EGAS00001005069:

  • Raw AML patient data (controlled access)
  • Available via University Health Network Genomics Data Access Committee

Zenodo Deposits:

  • Code for reproducing all analyses: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4683791
  • spiky package: https://doi.org/10.18129/B9.bioc.spiky


1.4 Differential Methylation Analysis Methodology

  • Exhaustive survey of DMA methods used with each assay type.
    • Not specific to Adela
  • Describe the analyis data in each step
  • Survey of benchmarking studies and tools


1.5 Enrichment-Based Differential Methylation Analysis

  • For enrichment-Based assays, a look at Bioinformatics Pipelines and Statistical Methods for Differential Methylation Analysis:
    • Common Bioinformatics Pipeline:FASTQ->BAN
    • DMA Methods for Enrichment based assays
      • many of the methods produce estimates of absolute beta, a measure of methylation level. These would then be further analyzed to get DMA results.


2 RF vs elastic net

  • RF vs elastic net: does RF edge enet and why?

  • From personal experience enet should do better with RF performance dropping substantially in the validation/evaliation set.
  • Also from Statistical learning with big data. A talk by Trevor Hastie (University of Bristol):
    • wide data - many features but few observations - calls for special methods to avoid overfitting. The elastic net is one of those methods.
    • tall data - many observations but reasonable number of features - not at risk of overfitting and can fit richer models with high orders of interactions.
  • Rerun the analyses which fit predictive models and compare RF and enet results

    • Halla-aho & Lähdesmäki (BMC Bioinformatics) [3]

    • RF is expected to lag in performance because the fitting dataset is not ruch enough to support the more complex RF models.

  • Word on feature selection - it is not needed here.
    • Predicting cancer is not a feature selection ploblem; it’s a predictive analysis problem.


3 Variability in cfMeDIP-seq Data

  • The key components of the assay - filler DNA and antibody instance - are associated with a considerable amount of variability.
    • docname provides a detailed look at the Methylated DNA Immunoprecipitation Stage of the protocol.
    • questions to address:
      • how does the filler DNA operate? where does the variability come from?
      • how does anti-5-methylcytosine (5mC) antibody work? where does the variablity come from?
      • can variability be attributed to its proper source - anti-5-methylcytosine (5mC) antibody or filler DNA?
  • Rerun the analyses which assess the performance of the spike-in controls.
    • Wilson et al. (2022) [4]


4 References

1.
Chen, K., Hu, Z., Xia, Z., Zhao, D., Li, W., and Tyler, J.K. (2015). The overlooked fact: Fundamental need for spike-in control for virtually all genome-wide analyses. Mol Cell Biol 36, 662–667.
2.
Wilson, S.L., Shen, S.Y., Harmon, L., Burgener, J.M., Triche, T.J., Bratman, S.V., De Carvalho, D.D., and Hoffman, M.M. (2022). Sensitive and reproducible cell-free methylome quantification with synthetic spike-in controls. Cell Rep Methods 2, 100294.
3.
Halla-aho, V., and Lähdesmäki, H. (2022). Probabilistic modeling methods for cell-free DNA methylation based cancer classification. BMC Bioinformatics 23, 138.
4.
Wilson, S.L., Shen, S.Y., Harmon, L., Burgener, J.M., Triche, T., Bratman, S.V., and De Carvalho, D.D. (2022). Sensitive and reproducible cell-free methylome quantification with synthetic spike-in controls. Cell Reports Methods 2, 100294.
